task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper news story for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of July 8, 2024. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: The National Grid Reliability Office opened a formal investigation on July 8, 2024, into a cascading grid failure that cut power to 3.4 million customers across four states on June 29.
The outage lasted an average of seven hours, with some rural areas without power for up to 18 hours.
Preliminary findings indicate a high-voltage transmission line owned by Stonegate Power tripped near Millbrook Junction due to contact with overgrown vegetation in 95-degree heat.
The initial line trip caused a rapid drop in grid frequency that triggered automatic protective relays at 14 neighboring substations to disconnect within 90 seconds.
The resulting imbalance between generation and load spread the outage from a single zone to a multi-state region faster than operators could intervene manually.

NGRO director Clara Osei said: "Automatic protection systems did exactly what they were designed to do — they protected equipment. What we're examining is why the cascade wasn't contained earlier in the sequence."

Stonegate Power vice president Martin Lund acknowledged the company's vegetation management inspections were last conducted in the affected corridor 22 months before the incident, exceeding the required 18-month interval.
The investigation will examine whether Stonegate's vegetation management non-compliance was known to regulators and whether existing penalties are sufficient to deter future lapses.
The June 29 event was the largest grid outage in the region since 2011.
Emergency generators at 12 hospitals in the affected area activated automatically; one hospital reported a brief generator startup failure that was restored within six minutes.
Estimated economic losses from the outage, including spoiled food, lost productivity, and emergency response costs, exceed $200 million according to a preliminary industry estimate.
The NGRO's investigation is expected to take six to nine months; the agency has authority to impose fines of up to $1 million per day per violation.
Grid frequency in North America is maintained at 60 hertz; deviations of as little as 0.5 hertz can trigger automatic equipment disconnections.
Power was restored to most urban customers within four hours after operators manually restarted generation sources in sequence to avoid a second cascade.
Three deaths have been tentatively attributed to the outage, including two people whose home medical equipment lost power; investigators have not yet confirmed causation.
Stonegate Power is the largest utility in the affected region, operating 8,400 kilometers of transmission lines across five states.
Industry analysts said vegetation management is responsible for more than a third of all major transmission outages in the past decade.
The NGRO has the authority to require utilities to submit corrective action plans within 60 days of a formal investigation finding.
Federal law prohibits utilities from passing investigation-related fines directly to ratepayers, though legal interpretations of that rule have varied.
Stonegate did not dispute the 22-month inspection gap but said the affected corridor was on a list for earlier inspection that was delayed by winter weather.

forbidden_additions: a confirmed causal link between the outage and the three deaths
a fine amount already issued by NGRO
a claim that Stonegate intentionally withheld inspection records
